ধরুন, ঢাকায় বসবাসকারী দুজন পেশাজীবী।প্রথমজন শুধু বাংলাদেশের চাকরির বিজ্ঞপ্তি দেখেন, CV জমা দেন এবং ইন্টারভিউয়ের অপেক্ষায় থাকেন। দ্বিতীয়জন 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐞𝐝𝐈𝐧-এ নিজের Professional Brand তৈরি করেন, আন্তর্জাতিক Recruiter-দের সঙ্গে যোগাযোগ করেন এবং Remote Jobs ও Global Clients খোঁজেন।

ছয় মাস পর তাঁদের সামনে তৈরি হওয়া সুযোগগুলো একেবারেই ভিন্ন হতে পারে। পার্থক্যটা সব সময় যোগ্যতায় নয়। অনেক সময় পার্থক্য তৈরি হয় সঠিক Positioning, Visibility এবং Networking-এর মাধ্যমে।

২০২৬ সালের বাস্তব তথ্য কী বলছে?

𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐞𝐝𝐈𝐧-এর প্রকাশিত গবেষণা অনুযায়ী:
■ 52% পেশাজীবী ২০২৬ সালে নতুন চাকরি খুঁজছেন।
■ 66% Recruiter যোগ্য প্রার্থী খুঁজে পেতে সমস্যার কথা জানিয়েছেন।
■ 93% Recruiter নিয়োগপ্রক্রিয়ায় AI-এর ব্যবহার বাড়ানোর পরিকল্পনা করছেন।
■ 59% Recruiter জানিয়েছেন, AI তাঁদের এমন যোগ্য প্রার্থী খুঁজে পেতে সাহায্য করছে, যাঁদের আগে হয়তো খুঁজে পেতেন না।

এবার ক্যারিয়ার গড়ার দুটি পদ্ধতির তুলনা করুন।
Traditional Job Search:
■ চাকরির বিজ্ঞপ্তি দেখা
■ CV জমা দেওয়া
■ ইন্টারভিউয়ের অপেক্ষা করা

Global Career Strategy:
■ International Remote Jobs খোঁজা
■ Recruiter ও Hiring Manager-এর সঙ্গে Networking
■ নিজের কাজ ও অর্জনের মাধ্যমে Credibility তৈরি
■ International Client Hunting
■ Global Business & Client Management

বাংলাদেশ থেকে কীভাবে সুযোগ তৈরি হতে পারে?
রাজশাহীর একজন Fresher নিজের Academic Projects ও Portfolio দিয়ে আন্তর্জাতিক Entry-Level Remote Position-এ আবেদন করতে পারেন। 

চট্টগ্রামের একজন অভিজ্ঞ Professional আন্তর্জাতিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের Remote Contract Role খুঁজতে পারেন। ঢাকার একজন Freelancer Marketplace-এর পাশাপাশি LinkedIn থেকে বিদেশি Business Owner-এর সঙ্গে সরাসরি যোগাযোগ করতে পারেন। Entrepreneur আন্তর্জাতিক Buyer, Client ও Business Partner-এর সঙ্গে সম্পর্ক তৈরি করতে পারেন।

একটি দেশে বসবাস করেও আন্তর্জাতিক ক্যারিয়ার গড়ার একাধিক পথ রয়েছে।

We posted a job. Then came the AI slop, impersonator and recruiter scam

Red flags that both job seekers and employers should watch for, in an era of AI slop and application scams

Andrew Losowsky  
The Markup 

“…Within 12 hours of posting the role, we received more than 400 applications. At first, most of these candidates seemed to be genuine. However, as the person who had to read them all, I quickly saw some red flags, which were all clear indicators of inauthenticity.

…I was curious about our probably fake applicants, so I followed up with some of them.

Several candidates said they had worked for PixelFyre Code Labs, “an information business helping all businesses succeed,” whose web address goes nowhere and seems only to exist on LinkedIn. One of them said he couldn’t discuss his past journalism work because “most of the work was under NDAs or white-label partnerships.” I tried to set up a phone call anyway, but he never responded to multiple emails. “Due to NDA” was a common refrain from suspect candidates when questioned about their experience.

…During the interview, the candidate’s answers were evasive and generic.

…Our job ad also got picked up and shared by scammers. Someone made a fake email address similar to ours, then sent generic technical “tests” containing our logo to jobseekers, while linking to our job ad. Completing these tests led to a fake contract signed by someone claiming to be our CEO – it was at this point that the scammers requested financial information, saying they needed it to issue payments. I shudder to think what would have happened to anyone who handed over their banking details. Based on what I know about AI, creating these scams at scale is probably pretty easy.”

𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐀𝐏𝐈 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐝𝐨 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬.

The business need gets documented. The team gets briefed. Everyone assumes the rest will figure itself out.

It does not.
Rate limits nobody asked about. Error responses in an unexpected format. Authentication different from what the requirement implied. Sandbox behaving nothing like the live environment.

Every one of those gaps is a BA gap, not a developer gap. Here is how to handle third party API integrations properly as a BA.

Understand the API before writing requirements.

1. Request vendor documentation immediately: Not to read it like a developer but to understand constraints, limitations, data formats, and authentication requirements before a single requirement is written.

2. Document the integration contract: Capture what data goes out, what comes back, and what each field means to the business process. This document sits between the business requirement and the technical implementation and saves hours of back and forth.

3. Define every error scenario explicitly:The happy path gets documented beautifully. Error states get left to developer judgment. Define the expected user experience for every failure.
- What happens when the API times out? 
- What does the user see when authentication fails?
- What happens when rate limits are hit at peak usage?
These are business decisions dressed as technical problems. The BA owns them.

4. Understand the vendor SLA:  If the API goes down in production who gets called? What is the expected resolution time? What fallback should the system show users? These questions belong in the requirements. Almost nobody asks them before go-live.

5. Flag sandbox validation as a testing requirement: Integrations that work perfectly in testing fail immediately in production when the sandbox does not reflect live API behaviour. Explicitly require that sandbox and production behaviour are validated before sign-off.

🐉🔥 Apparently, asking questions before quitting your job is “too much.”

Recently, a company co-founder offered me ₹45,000/month for a work-from-home role — 10 hours a day, 6 days a week — and expected me to leave my current job.

Before making that decision, I asked for clarity.

Not unreasonable demands.

Basic questions.

Is this employment or a contract?

Would I ever be required to travel to the office?

What is the legal company name and office address?

How will TDS/PF/ESI work?

When is salary credited?

What are the working hours, overtime rules, leave policy, probation and notice period?

Who provides the laptop and paid AI/video tools?

Can I continue occasional freelance/promotional work and my own social-media projects outside office hours?

How will my performance be evaluated?

In total, I asked 14 questions.

And that became the problem.

The tone changed.

The irritation became obvious.

The conversation became increasingly informal and dismissive simply because I wanted clarity before resigning from an existing job.

So I declined the offer.

🐉🔥

Here is something hiring companies need to understand:

An offer is not a favour being granted to a candidate.

If you are asking someone to resign from their existing employment and commit most of their week to your company, they have every right to understand exactly what they are signing up for.

Questions about salary, workload, leave, contracts, equipment, outside work and evaluation are not signs of a “difficult employee.”

They are signs of an informed professional.

In fact, if reasonable questions irritate an employer before Day 1, that reaction itself provides useful information about what Day 100 might look like.

Candidates should evaluate employers too.

Have you ever had an employer become uncomfortable simply because you asked detailed questions before accepting an offer? 🐉🔥

If you freelance from Nigeria and get paid in dollars, one rule changed on January 1, 2026 that most freelance advice hasn't caught up with.
Nigerian tax residents are now taxed on worldwide income, including foreign freelance earnings from platforms like Upwork and Fiverr.
(Confirm your own situation with the Nigeria Revenue Service or a licensed accountant. But "nobody checks foreign income" is no longer a safe assumption.)
That was one of five findings from researching a guide for beginner freelancers outside the major Western markets:
1. PayPal now works in Nigeria through a Paga partnership (January 2026). Advice saying it doesn't is outdated.
2. Generic AI task work is growing in volume but paying less per contract. Upwork's 2026 research found volume up about 90% while pay per contract fell 13%. Knowing ChatGPT is not a moat.
3. AI tools confidently invent facts about real people and companies. OpenAI's own testing found its reasoning models got person-specific questions wrong roughly a third to half the time. Verify before you put a "personalized" fact in a pitch.
4. Location bias in freelance hiring is measured, not imagined. Published research found it, and also found that verified proof helps, though it doesn't fully close the gap.
5. Needing the work does not mean you should quote low. Research on negotiation found that a weak fallback offer drags your opening number down more than having no alternative at all.
I put these into a 20-chapter guide: The First International Client System. Every chapter ends with its sources, and where my own checking caught an error, the correction stays visible in the text.
It does not promise clients or income. It gives you a process: validate the problem, build proof, earn trust, price, pitch, contract, get paid.

A recruiter sent me a role this week that has stayed with me. It was a three month contract, described as guaranteed through the end of the year, with the possibility of extension if the person proved their value. Inside the description were three different jobs: someone to build and ship hands-on data and integration work, someone to independently review the architecture and governance of an AI strategy, and someone to write the enterprise roadmap for the year ahead.

Any one of those is a real engagement. Together they describe a hope more than a role.

What interests me is the system that produces a posting like this. When an organization has not yet decided what it actually needs, the ambiguity has to land somewhere, and it usually lands on the person hired to absorb it. The word guaranteed sits beside the phrase prove your value, and the risk quietly moves from the company to the contractor. Nobody in the chain is acting badly. The structure is simply doing what it was built to do.

The better question for any organization is what outcome it wants and which of the three jobs comes first. Build, assess, and plan are different kinds of work, and they deserve to be scoped, sequenced, and paid as such. Clarity at the beginning costs very little, and its absence tends to get billed later in some other form.

This is what is wrong with our world right now. People are struggling to find jobs, and too many companies are taking advantage of that.

I passed on this one, kindly. If you are hiring for something like it, start by separating the jobs.

Layoffs are down 41%.

Hiring is back to 2013 levels.

Both are true. Only one makes the headlines.

The numbers:
→ Announced job cuts through August: down 41% (Challenger, Gray & Christmas)
→ Hiring rate: 3.3%, roughly where it was in 2013 (BLS JOLTS)
→ Quit rate: 1.9%. People with jobs aren't leaving.
→ Job openings: a five-month low in August
→ #1 reason given for cuts this year: AI. 116,175 jobs, 22% of the total.

Economists call this a "low-hire, low-fire" market.

Picture a building with a locked front door. Almost no one is being pushed out. Almost no one is getting in.

The Cleveland Fed found those hit hardest are job seekers who aren't currently employed. That's why the jobs report and your search feel like two different economies.

This is the Great Restructuring.

Companies aren't just cutting. They're redesigning how work gets done:
→ Fewer full-time roles
→ More contract and project-based work
→ Flatter teams with fewer managers
→ Budget moved from headcount to AI

Why? In a UK survey of 1,000+ business leaders, 39% have scaled back full-time hiring. Their top reasons: flexibility (49%) and avoiding long-term commitments (43%). Only 34% said cost.

It's not just about saving money. It's about never being locked in again.

Where the cuts are concentrated this year:
→ Technology: 155,126, nearly 30% of all cuts
→ Transportation: up 271% from 2025

The cost no jobs report measures:
For candidates:
→ Hundreds of applications, very few replies
→ Savings shrinking while the search stretches on
→ Starting to doubt skills that were in demand two years ago

For employees who still have jobs:
→ Survivor's guilt after watching colleagues get cut

🎬 Meet Dave, Head of Talent
The CFO asked why they're paying recruiters 15–20% of salary, & Dave had an idea 🤔💡 "We'll hire specialists ourselves. We've got AI now" 👀

Recruiter's contract was cancelled, their role is "on hold due to restructuring"

Week 1. Dave posts for a Head of Cyber Security. The requirements are 10+ years in agentic AI (the tech is 3 years old), a "digital native," and a "young, dynamic culture" It pays 2014 rates.

Week 2. 4,000+ applications arrive. AI wrote most of them. AI screens all of them in 0.4 seconds.

The ATS, trained on a decade of Dave's past decisions, rejects:
🚩 the 25+ yr veteran, for being "overqualified"
🚩 the person who red teamed new systems before most launched, for not being "a digital native", tested the internet before the hiring manager had email. "Digital native" = code for too old, and unlawful to say aloud.
🚩 the graduate, for "not enough experience" for an entry role needing 5 yrs

Week 4. The shortlist is the 26 yr old who listed ChatGPT as a core competency + 3 people who don't exist.

Week 5. Silence. Dave's LinkedIn banner says "We're hiring!” 🚀 The only people reading the job ad closely are attackers mapping Dave's tech stack🕵️

Week 6. Candidates bare their souls to an interview bot that isn't hiring. Nobody hears back, LinkedIn notices.

Week 7. Dave pivots & decides to "just get a contractor" AI benchmarks the day rate against 2019 data, offshore averages, & a chatbot's best guess, so the ad offers a "competitive rate" for 12 mths with no extensions. Specialists read that as half the rate for twice the scope, & none of them reply. The only taker's LinkedIn says "Cyber | Crypto | Life Coach."

Week 9. The CFO asks where the hire is. Dave says "The role went via an alternative route"

Week 10. Scammers spot the gap. They WhatsApp Dave's ghosted candidates "from" his company, offer the job, ask for passport & bank details. Finally, someone replied.

Week 12. There's a breach, & no CISO / security lead. Dave hires an emergency incident responder at triple the day rate he refused in Week 7. Meanwhile, the ghosted veteran is now advising a competitor & sits on your procurement panel.

That 15–20% recruitment fee is looking cheap.

The U.S. has suspended PERM processing for Microsoft, Adobe and several major IT-services firms, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and Cognizant.

PERM is a key step in employer-sponsored permanent residency. Suspending it creates uncertainty for affected foreign workers and limits an important recruitment and retention pathway for these companies.

We are hiring for the role of AI Full Stack Engineer (Azure). Please share resumes at Akanksha@mcubesoft.com

AI Full Stack Engineer (Azure) 
Location : Remote 

You will join a small, dedicated team supporting and evolving a commercial AI chatbot platform for a US pharmaceutical client. The platform is live, serving a field sales organization, and built on Python FastAPI, React, and multi-agent LLM orchestration running on Azure Container Apps. The work is a mix of production support, feature engineering, and platform operations. You will own delivery end to end within the clients existing Azure DevOps environment. What You Will Do Application engineering (primary) • Maintain and extend the FastAPI backend and React/TypeScript frontend • Develop and support multi-agent workflows: intent routing, product Qamp;A;, field scheduling, and analytics • Maintain compliance controls, policy enforcement, and audit logging • Support integrations with Microsoft Graph/Outlook, Veeva/Salesforce (OBO flows), and Microsoft Fabric • Manage the Markdown-based knowledge retrieval pipeline • Investigate and resolve production incidents from Sev 1 through Sev 4 within agreed SLAs • Deliver features from requirement through peer-reviewed PR, test, and release Platform operations (secondary, as needed) • Operate Azure Container Apps across Dev, QA, and Production: deployments, revision management, rollback • Maintain Azure DevOps YAML pipelines and Bicep infrastructure definitions • Manage Key Vault, Managed Identity, and secrets governance • Configure and maintain Application Insights, Log Analytics, and Azure Monitor alerting What You Need • 6+ years in software engineering with Python and TypeScript/React as primary skills • Production experience building or operating agentic or LLM-based system • Working knowledge of Azure Container Apps, Key Vault, Managed Identity, and Azure DevOps pipelines • Familiarity with Microsoft Entra ID and MSAL authentication flows • Comfortable operating in a regulated environment with change governance and PR-gated deployments • US-based; available during US Central Time business hours Preferred • Azure certification: Developer Associate, Solutions Architect Expert, or DevOps Engineer Expert • Experience with Anthropic Claude API or comparable LLM APIs • Familiarity with Veeva CRM, Salesforce Apex, or Microsoft Graph integrations • Prior work in pharma, life sciences, or commercial operations platforms

#AI#FullStackEngineer#Azure#Contract#C2C#W2#LLM#API
